body.p: I read with great interest the recent study by Omohwovo 1 on wastewater management challenges in Africa, which has strong parallels with the Philippines’ own struggles in this area. Like Africa, our country is experiencing rapid population growth and urbanization without the necessary infrastructure to support effective wastewater treatment. The Philippines is also facing poor wastewater management that has led to severe heath concerns for humans, animals, and ecosystem. Since wastewater treatment and disposal facilities are rare, domestic wastewater is discharged without treatment. 2 This has resulted in serious public health risks and environmental damage—problems that mirror those highlighted in Africa and emphasize the urgency of meeting the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal 6 (SDG 6) for clean water and sanitation. This paper aims to provide guidelines for the Philippine government to consider localized solutions and policy integration to solve the issue of wastewater management in the Philippines.

In the Philippines, only 10% of wastewater is treated while 58% of the groundwater is contaminated while 5% of the total population is connected to a sewer network. The vast majority uses flush toilets connected to septic tanks. Metro Manila alone generates about 2 million cubic meters of wastewater every day. 3 Untreated wastewater contributes to the spread of waterborne diseases like diarrhea, cholera, and leptospirosis, hitting marginalized communities hardest. These areas often lack adequate healthcare and sanitation facilities, making them particularly vulnerable. 2

The Philippine government’s efforts to achieve universal coverage of water and sanitation services by 2028 will necessitate the adoption of sustainable strategies to facilitate this transition. 3 There is a need for a complete review and overhaul of wastewater management policies, especially regarding septage management. One must adopt a broader perspective that incorporates life cycle thinking in wastewater treatment, weighing both ecological benefits and climate impacts. Locally solutions and low-cost wastewater treatment technologies are crucial, especially for rural and underserved urban areas. For example, the use of decentralized treatment systems and Constructed Wetlands (CWs) are examples of effective, low-cost Nature-based Solutions (NbS) that can be prioritized. 4 In the context of smart cities, advanced wastewater management systems equipped with sensors can play a crucial role in addressing freshwater demand by detecting and mitigating combined sewage overflows and chemical pollutants in wastewater. Moreover, wastewater treatment offers an opportunity to maximize the reuse of water resources, enabling their repeated utilization. 3

Although the Clean Water Act of 2004 or Republic Act No. 9275 provides a framework for managing wastewater in the Philippines, its implementation is far from robust. Stronger government oversight, tighter enforcement of regulations, and increased collaboration between public and private sectors are needed to achieve real progress. Local water quality benchmarks should be established, and penalties for non-compliance must be enforced to ensure accountability. Training programs for operators of wastewater facilities, as well as support for local governments, can improve system efficiency. Public education campaigns are also vital to boost community participation in proper waste disposal and water conservation. 5

The Philippines’ susceptibility to typhoons and severe weather only complicates matters further. Our wastewater infrastructure needs to be resilient to these events to prevent untreated sewage from polluting water sources. 6 After Typhoon Haiyan, 44% of collected water samples were contaminated just 3 weeks post-disaster. Ten months later, contamination remained widespread, with 65% of samples testing positive for E. coli. Contamination was not confined to any single part of the drinking-water system; it affected 70% of water sources, 67% of storage facilities, and 57% of distribution systems. This highlights the need for resilient infrastructure that can withstand the impacts of climate change. 7

Looking ahead, there is a clear need for innovative research and adaptive strategies in the Philippines’ wastewater sector. 8 Community-based wastewater treatment systems should be evaluated for their practicality in remote and disadvantaged areas. The concept of treating wastewater as a valuable resource is another promising avenue: energy recovery, nutrient recycling, and biogas production are all potential benefits that can be tapped. Cultural and socioeconomic factors also play a role in shaping wastewater management practices and should be explored to encourage broader community engagement. Additionally, the long-term effects of climate change on wastewater infrastructure and water quality must be studied to inform future disaster planning. 8

In tackling these complex challenges, Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are an exciting area of promise. 4 Constructed Wetlands (CWs), for example, offer an effective, eco-friendly means of treating wastewater and ensuring water security. Implementing such solutions requires a comprehensive, integrated approach—one that combines local knowledge, strong governance, public education, and international best practices.

Achieving a sustainable future in the Philippines requires transforming wastewater from a threat into an opportunity. These innovations should prioritize addressing genuine, pressing societal challenges and delivering tangible benefits that enhance the quality of life of Filipinos. This shift will protect public health, preserve our environment, and contribute to the nation’s progress toward meeting sustainable development goals. It is a call to action for policymakers, communities, and researchers to come together in creating resilient, localized wastewater solutions that serve both people and the planet.
